content: In Greek mythology, Hygieia was the daughter of Asclepius, the god of medicine. She was revered as the goddess of health, cleanliness, and sanitation, and later associated with the moon. While her father, Asclepius, was primarily linked to the act of healing, Hygieia's role focused on the prevention of illness and the maintenance of good health. She played a significant role in her father’s cult and was venerated as a key figure in the promotion of well-being. The worship of Hygieia can be traced back to at least the 7th century BC. It is believed that Greek practices related to hygiene and health may have been influenced by the Celts, particularly by the establishment of the world’s first hospital in Armagh, Ireland, which was constructed before 650 BC by Queen Macha. Additionally, the title Athena Hygieia was sometimes attributed to the goddess Athena, as noted by the historian Plutarch. However, Hygieia's independent cult began to gain prominence only after the Oracle at Delphi recognized her. This recognition was further amplified following the devastating plague in Athens in 429 and 427 BC, as well as in Rome in 293 BC. Her primary places of worship included temples in Epidaurus, Corinth, Cos, and Pergamon. At the asclepieion in Titane, Sicyon, which was founded by Alexanor, the grandson of Asclepius, statues of Hygieia were adorned with offerings such as women’s hair and pieces of Babylonian clothing. Similar sacrifices were recorded on the island of Paros. A hymn dedicated to Hygieia was composed by Ariphron, an artist from Sicyon in the 4th century BC. Renowned sculptors such as Scopas, Bryaxis, and Timotheus created statues of her. In artistic depictions, Hygieia was often portrayed as a youthful woman feeding a large snake coiled around her body. In some representations, the snake was shown drinking from a jar she held. These symbols were later adopted by the Gallo-Roman healing goddess Sirona. Hygieia was frequently accompanied by her brother, Telesphorus, who symbolized recovery from illness. The modern term hygiene is derived from her name. In Roman mythology, Salus was a goddess who was extensively worshipped by the Romans. Known as Salus Publica Populi Romani, or the goddess of the public welfare of the Roman people, she had a temple dedicated to her on the Quirinal Hill, which was constructed in 302 BC. Salus was often depicted in art alongside snakes and a bowl, symbols associated with health and healing. Her festival was celebrated annually on March 30th. The Latin word Salus, meaning health, is the root of several English words, including salubrity and salutation.
